claim: Recent phylogenetic analyses indicate that RNA virus populations carry a significant deleterious mutation load.
source: Recent phylogenetic analyses indicate that RNA virus populations carry a significant deleterious mutation load.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research in the field.

claim: Deleterious mutations act to slow the virus's rate of antigenic evolution.
source: By first analyzing simple models of influenza that incorporate a mutation load, we show that deleterious mutations, as expected, act to slow the virus's rate of antigenic evolution, while making it more punctuated in nature.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations and analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Deleterious mutations make antigenic evolution more punctuated in nature.
source: By first analyzing simple models of influenza that incorporate a mutation load, we show that deleterious mutations, as expected, act to slow the virus's rate of antigenic evolution, while making it more punctuated in nature.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations and analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: The models predict three distinct molecular pathways by which antigenic cluster transitions occur.
source: These models further predict three distinct molecular pathways by which antigenic cluster transitions occur, and we find phylogenetic patterns consistent with each of these pathways in influenza virus sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by model predictions and phylogenetic analyses of influenza sequences.

claim: Phylogenetic patterns consistent with each of the three predicted molecular pathways are found in influenza virus sequences.
source: These models further predict three distinct molecular pathways by which antigenic cluster transitions occur, and we find phylogenetic patterns consistent with each of these pathways in influenza virus sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analyses of influenza sequences presented in the manuscript.

claim: Antigenic mutations act in concert with deleterious mutations to reproduce influenza's spindly hemagglutinin phylogeny.
source: Simulations of a more complex phylodynamic model further indicate that antigenic mutations act in concert with deleterious mutations to reproduce influenza's spindly hemagglutinin phylogeny, co-circulation of antigenic variants, and high annual attack rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylodynamic model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Antigenic mutations act in concert with deleterious mutations to reproduce co-circulation of antigenic variants.
source: Simulations of a more complex phylodynamic model further indicate that antigenic mutations act in concert with deleterious mutations to reproduce influenza's spindly hemagglutinin phylogeny, co-circulation of antigenic variants, and high annual attack rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylodynamic model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Antigenic mutations act in concert with deleterious mutations to reproduce high annual attack rates.
source: Simulations of a more complex phylodynamic model further indicate that antigenic mutations act in concert with deleterious mutations to reproduce influenza's spindly hemagglutinin phylogeny, co-circulation of antigenic variants, and high annual attack rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylodynamic model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Seasonal influenza viruses infect up to 15% of the world's human population annually.
source: Seasonal influenza viruses infect up to 15% of the world's human population annually, with the majority of flu cases attributable to influenza type A subtype H3N2 (A/H3N2) (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization.

claim: The majority of flu cases are attributable to influenza type A subtype H3N2 (A/H3N2).
source: Seasonal influenza viruses infect up to 15% of the world's human population annually, with the majority of flu cases attributable to influenza type A subtype H3N2 (A/H3N2) (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization.

claim: Influenza A/H3N2 in humans carries a deleterious mutation load.
source: Distinct from these efforts, several phylogenetic analyses have indicated that influenza A/H3N2 in humans carries a deleterious mutation load (Fitch et al., 1997; Pybus et al., 2007; Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple phylogenetic analyses.

claim: Fitch et al. (1997) found the number of nonsynonymous changes on tip branches of the HA phylogeny to be higher than expected.
source: Specifically, early work by Fitch et al. (1997) found the number of nonsynonymous changes on tip branches of the HA phylogeny to be higher than expected, indicative of either strain selection bias or the presence of transiently circulating deleterious mutations in the influenza viral population.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fitch et al. (1997).

claim: Higher than expected nonsynonymous changes on tip branches is indicative of either strain selection bias or the presence of transiently circulating deleterious mutations.
source: Specifically, early work by Fitch et al. (1997) found the number of nonsynonymous changes on tip branches of the HA phylogeny to be higher than expected, indicative of either strain selection bias or the presence of transiently circulating deleterious mutations in the influenza viral population.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from phylogenetic patterns and cited work.

claim: Pybus et al. (2007) found heightened ratios of non-synonymous-to-synonymous substitutions on external tree branches relative to those found internally for H3N2's M1 protein.
source: In more recent work, Pybus et al. (2007) performed a comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of over 140 viruses, including influenza A/H3N2. For H3N2's M1 protein, as well as for the majority of the other viral proteins examined in the study, they found heightened ratios of non-synonymous-to-synonymous substitutions on external tree branches relative to those found internally.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pybus et al. (2007).

claim: Heightened ratios of non-synonymous-to-synonymous substitutions on external tree branches points towards transiently circulating deleterious mutations in influenza and across RNA virus populations.
source: This finding again points towards transiently circulating deleterious mutations in influenza and, more generally, across RNA virus populations.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from phylogenetic patterns and cited work.

claim: Accounting for fitness costs associated with sublethal deleterious mutations is necessary when projecting the frequencies of influenza clades into the next season.
source: Other recent work on predicting the short-term evolution of influenza has highlighted the necessity of accounting for fitness costs associated with sublethal deleterious mutations when projecting the frequencies of influenza clades into the next season (Łuksza and Lässig, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Łuksza and Lässig (2014).

claim: Purifying selection is not sufficiently strong to immediately eliminate deleterious mutations from the influenza A/H3N2 virus population that circulates among humans.
source: Together, these results indicate that purifying selection is not sufficiently strong to immediately eliminate deleterious mutations from the influenza A/H3N2 virus population that circulates among humans.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple cited studies.

claim: Deleterious mutations have the potential to interact with beneficial mutations in determining which viral lineages will persist and which ones will ultimately be lost.
source: As a result of genetic linkage within genes and, to a lesser extent, across genes, these deleterious mutations have the potential to interact with beneficial mutations in determining which viral lineages will persist and which ones will ultimately be lost.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from population genetic theory.

claim: Interference effects largely determine the fates of viral mutants in influenza A/H3N2, rather than their inherent selective effects.
source: Indeed, a recent statistical analysis of HA sequences from influenza A/H3N2 has suggested that interference effects largely determine the fates of viral mutants, rather than their inherent selective effects (Illingworth and Mustonen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Illingworth and Mustonen (2012).

claim: There is extensive genetic linkage across influenza's HA.
source: These interference effects are possible because of an extensive genetic linkage across influenza's HA (Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012) and arise from variation in the background fitness of viral strains and from variation in the fitness effects of subsequent mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Strelkowa and Lässig (2012).

claim: Sublethal deleterious mutations commonly arise and circulate for sufficiently long periods of time to be able to impact the trajectories of influenza A/H3N2 strains.
source: Taken together, this body of work indicates that sublethal deleterious mutations commonly arise and circulate for sufficiently long periods of time to be able to impact the trajectories of influenza A/H3N2 strains.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from multiple cited studies.

claim: Circulating sublethal deleterious mutations in influenza A/H3N2's viral population reduce the rate of adaptive evolution.
source: As expected from previous analyses of these types of models (Fisher, 1930; Birky and Walsh, 1988; Peck, 1994; Barton, 1995; Orr, 2000), we find that circulating sublethal deleterious mutations in influenza A/H3N2's viral population reduce the rate of adaptive evolution and increase the average size of the beneficial mutants that fix.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results and citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Circulating sublethal deleterious mutations increase the average size of the beneficial mutants that fix.
source: As expected from previous analyses of these types of models (Fisher, 1930; Birky and Walsh, 1988; Peck, 1994; Barton, 1995; Orr, 2000), we find that circulating sublethal deleterious mutations in influenza A/H3N2's viral population reduce the rate of adaptive evolution and increase the average size of the beneficial mutants that fix.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results and citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The accumulation of deleterious mutations can contribute to explaining the invasion dynamics of new antigenic clusters.
source: Extending this analysis to models explicitly incorporating epidemiological dynamics, we further show that the accumulation of deleterious mutations can contribute to explaining the invasion dynamics of new antigenic clusters, defined as sets of viral strains that are antigenically similar to one another (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by model results and a citation defining antigenic clusters.

claim: The virus population at epidemiological equilibrium will have an overall net reproductive rate (i.e., mean absolute fitness) of R = 1.
source: The virus population at epidemiological equilibrium will have an overall net reproductive rate (i.e., mean absolute fitness) of R = 1, with more transmissible viruses that carry fewer deleterious mutations having reproductive rates above one and less transmissible viruses that carry more deleterious mutations having reproductive rates below one (Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by model results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: More transmissible viruses that carry fewer deleterious mutations have reproductive rates above one.
source: The virus population at epidemiological equilibrium will have an overall net reproductive rate (i.e., mean absolute fitness) of R = 1, with more transmissible viruses that carry fewer deleterious mutations having reproductive rates above one and less transmissible viruses that carry more deleterious mutations having reproductive rates below one (Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by model results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Less transmissible viruses that carry more deleterious mutations have reproductive rates below one.
source: The virus population at epidemiological equilibrium will have an overall net reproductive rate (i.e., mean absolute fitness) of R = 1, with more transmissible viruses that carry fewer deleterious mutations having reproductive rates above one and less transmissible viruses that carry more deleterious mutations having reproductive rates below one (Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by model results shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Antigenic mutants experience one of three possible fates: rapid loss, transient circulation, or successful establishment.
source: Antigenic mutants therefore experience one of three possible fates (Figure 1B): rapid loss, transient circulation, or successful establishment.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The lower the number of background deleterious mutations, the higher the antigenic mutant's chances are of at least transient establishment.
source: Which of these three fates awaits an antigenic mutant depends in part on the number of deleterious mutations carried by the strain in which the antigenic mutation arises: the lower the number of background deleterious mutations, the higher the antigenic mutant's chances are of at least transient establishment, consistent with the background fitness interference effects found in Illingworth and Mustonen (2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by model results and a citation to Illingworth and Mustonen (2012).

claim: The vast majority of small-sized antigenic mutants are rapidly lost.
source: The vast majority of small-sized antigenic mutants are rapidly lost; the remaining ones only circulate transiently before the accumulation of deleterious mutations results in their ultimate loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results.

claim: Small-sized antigenic mutants that are not rapidly lost only circulate transiently before the accumulation of deleterious mutations results in their ultimate loss.
source: The vast majority of small-sized antigenic mutants are rapidly lost; the remaining ones only circulate transiently before the accumulation of deleterious mutations results in their ultimate loss.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results.

claim: Antigenic mutants that significantly escape immunity are less subject to rapid loss and also less likely to circulate only transiently.
source: Antigenic mutants that significantly escape immunity are less subject to rapid loss and also less likely to circulate only transiently.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results.

claim: The average size of antigenic mutations that will successfully establish increases with increases in the deleterious mutation rate λ.
source: Figure 1D shows that this average antigenic size increases with increases in the deleterious mutation rate λ.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: For any given deleterious mutation rate λ, as sd decreases the average size of antigenic mutants that will successfully establish increases.
source: For any given deleterious mutation rate λ, as sd decreases the average size of antigenic mutants that fix increases (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by model results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Increases in λ and decreases in sd similarly increase the virus population's fitness variance.
source: These results can be interpreted in the context of findings from the population genetics literature: increases in λ and decreases in sd similarly increase the virus population's fitness variance (as quantified by the variance in net reproductive rate R, Figure 1A inset, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This claim is supported by model results and population genetics theory.

claim: Increases in the fitness variance of asexual populations makes fixation of a beneficial mutant increasingly dependent on genetic background.
source: Increases in the fitness variance of asexual populations makes fixation of a beneficial mutant increasingly dependent on genetic background; only beneficial mutants that exceed a characteristic large size will have a high probability of fixing in populations with substantial fitness variance (Peck, 1994; Barton, 1995; Schiffels et al., 2011; Good et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to population genetics literature.

claim: Only beneficial mutants that exceed a characteristic large size will have a high probability of fixing in populations with substantial fitness variance.
source: Increases in the fitness variance of asexual populations makes fixation of a beneficial mutant increasingly dependent on genetic background; only beneficial mutants that exceed a characteristic large size will have a high probability of fixing in populations with substantial fitness variance (Peck, 1994; Barton, 1995; Schiffels et al., 2011; Good et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to population genetics literature.

claim: Circulating deleterious mutations act to slow the tempo of antigenic evolution.
source: In addition to their effect on the sizes of successfully establishing antigenic mutants, circulating deleterious mutations will act to slow the tempo of antigenic evolution (Figure 1E); that is, they will reduce the number of antigenic mutants that go to fixation in a given amount of time.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Increases in the deleterious mutation rate λ and decreases in the fitness cost of deleterious mutations sd similarly act to increase fitness variance.
source: Again, increases in the fitness variance of the viral population is the culprit: increases in the deleterious mutation rate λ and decreases in the fitness cost of deleterious mutations sd similarly act to increase fitness variance; with increased fitness variance in the population, the genetic background in which an antigenic mutant needs to arise in to have a chance at fixation will be increasingly restrictive.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results and population genetics theory.

claim: With increased fitness variance in the population, the genetic background in which an antigenic mutant needs to arise in to have a chance at fixation will be increasingly restrictive.
source: Again, increases in the fitness variance of the viral population is the culprit: increases in the deleterious mutation rate λ and decreases in the fitness cost of deleterious mutations sd similarly act to increase fitness variance; with increased fitness variance in the population, the genetic background in which an antigenic mutant needs to arise in to have a chance at fixation will be increasingly restrictive.
evidence: This claim is supported by model results and population genetics theory.

claim: Influenza A/H3N2 undergoes punctuated antigenic evolution.
source: In particular, detailed antigenic analyses have demonstrated that this virus undergoes punctuated antigenic evolution, with predominantly single amino acid changes of large antigenic effect being responsible for the occurrence of antigenic cluster transitions (Smith et al., 2004; Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to antigenic analyses.

claim: Predominantly single amino acid changes of large antigenic effect are responsible for the occurrence of antigenic cluster transitions.
source: In particular, detailed antigenic analyses have demonstrated that this virus undergoes punctuated antigenic evolution, with predominantly single amino acid changes of large antigenic effect being responsible for the occurrence of antigenic cluster transitions (Smith et al., 2004; Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to antigenic analyses.

claim: Antigenic cluster transitions occur only every 2 to 6 years.
source: These same analyses, as well as others (Plotkin et al., 2002), have further indicated that antigenic cluster transitions occur only every 2 to 6 years, an incredibly slow pace given the virus's high mutation rate and the need for only a single amino acid to substantially alter antigenicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to antigenic analyses.

claim: The punctuated and surprisingly slow nature of influenza A/H3N2's antigenic evolution are related features of this largely asexual, adapting population subject to a deleterious mutation load.
source: Thus, our model posits that the punctuated and surprisingly slow nature of influenza A/H3N2's antigenic evolution are related features of this largely asexual, adapting population subject to a deleterious mutation load: adaptive evolution requires not only that large antigenic mutants occur, but also that they occur in good genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model results.

claim: Adaptive evolution requires not only that large antigenic mutants occur, but also that they occur in good genetic backgrounds.
source: Thus, our model posits that the punctuated and surprisingly slow nature of influenza A/H3N2's antigenic evolution are related features of this largely asexual, adapting population subject to a deleterious mutation load: adaptive evolution requires not only that large antigenic mutants occur, but also that they occur in good genetic backgrounds.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model results.

claim: Small antigenic mutants arising in low-load ('good') genetic backgrounds transiently circulate.
source: Transient circulation occurs when a small antigenic mutant arises in a good genetic background (Figure 2A), provided that it survived genetic drift.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Small antigenic mutants arising in average genetic backgrounds are rapidly lost.
source: Rapid loss is expected to occur when a small antigenic mutant arises in an average genetic background (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Large antigenic mutants arising in good genetic backgrounds can successfully establish and exclude the resident antigenic strain.
source: Successful establishment can only occur when a large antigenic mutation arises in a good genetic background (Figure 2C), a 'jackpot' combination. In this case, the resident strain is competitively excluded as a result of strain cross-immunity.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Large antigenic mutants arising in average genetic backgrounds transiently circulate.
source: Transient circulation also occurs when a large antigenic mutant arises in an average genetic background (Figure 2D), again provided that it survived genetic drift.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The presence of deleterious mutations can affect the invasion dynamics of antigenic mutants having the 'jackpot' combination.
source: Intriguingly, the presence of deleterious mutations can also affect the invasion dynamics of antigenic mutants having this 'jackpot' combination: because offspring of antigenic mutants accumulate deleterious mutations, and these deleterious mutations reduce viral transmissibility, the invasion dynamics of particularly large antigenic mutants are considerably less explosive than would be expected in the absence of deleterious mutation accumulation (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: Large antigenic mutants do not readily burn themselves out during attempted establishment.
source: Consequently, large antigenic mutants do not readily burn themselves out during attempted establishment, as might in theory be expected (Ballesteros et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations and a citation.

claim: The BE92-to-WU95 cluster transition was precipitated by an amino acid change from N to K at site 145.
source: The BE92-to-WU95 cluster transition, precipitated by an amino acid change from N to K at site 145, is a good example of a cluster transition occurring via a single mutational step (Koel et al., 2013) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koel et al. (2013) and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Several clades witnessed the 145NK amino acid substitution before it occurred in the clade that founded the WU95 viral lineage.
source: Of note, several clades witnessed the 145NK amino acid substitution before it occurred in the clade that founded the WU95 viral lineage.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The failure of early 145K clades to establish could in principle be a consequence of this N-to-K amino acid change occurring in insufficiently good genetic backgrounds.
source: Our models above indicate that the failure of these early 145K clades to establish could in principle be a consequence of this N-to-K amino acid change occurring in insufficiently good genetic backgrounds, as also suggested in Neher et al. (2014).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model results and a citation.

claim: All three of the largest 145K clades that failed to establish were geographically widespread, spanning at least two continents.
source: We thus examined the spatial locations of the sequences from the three largest 145K clades that failed to establish: all three clades were geographically widespread, spanning at least two continents.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of sequence data.

claim: Two of the three largest 145K clades that failed to establish contained sequences from Asia.
source: Furthermore, two of the three clades contained sequences from Asia, despite Asia being undersampled during this time period.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of sequence data.

claim: It is unlikely that the early 145K clades were geographically restricted to 'sink' populations.
source: It is thus unlikely that these early 145K clades were geographically restricted to 'sink' populations.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from geographic distribution data.

claim: The WU95-SY97 antigenic cluster transition required two amino acid changes (156KQ and 158EK).
source: Hemagglutination inhibition assays experimentally indicated that two amino acid changes (156KQ and 158EK) were necessary to precipitate the cluster transition (Koel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to experimental work by Koel et al. (2013).

claim: The WU95-SY97 cluster transition shows evolutionary dynamics consistent with the two-step antigenic change molecular pathway.
source: A phylogenetic analysis of the WU95-SY97 antigenic cluster transition provides an empirical example that is consistent with this molecular pathway of antigenic turnover, with a seemingly simultaneous accumulation of two antigenic amino acid changes (156KQ and 158EK) occurring on a short branch of the reconstructed phylogeny (Koel et al., 2013) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4B and a citation.

claim: A virus antigenically characterized as FU02 reassorted with a genetically distant virus antigenically characterized as SY97 during the SY97-FU02 cluster transition.
source: A phylogenetic analysis of the SY97-FU02 cluster transition provides an especially compelling example that is consistent with this molecular pathway of antigenic turnover. In this cluster transition, a virus antigenically characterized as FU02 reassorted with a genetically distant virus antigenically characterized as SY97 (Barr et al., 2005; Holmes et al., 2005) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4C and citations.

claim: The FU02 reassortant viral lineage circulated extensively in Australia and New Zealand in 2003 and subsequently in the US in the 2003–2004 influenza season, causing substantial morbidity and mortality.
source: This reassortant viral lineage circulated extensively in Australia and New Zealand in 2003 and subsequently in the US in the 2003–2004 influenza season, causing substantial morbidity and mortality (Barr et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barr et al. (2005).

claim: The CA04 lineage carried not only an HA mutation of large antigenic size, but also two amino acid changes in its polymerase gene segment that enhanced replicative fitness.
source: Intriguingly, the CA04 lineage carried with it not only an HA mutation of large antigenic size, but also two amino acid changes in its polymerase gene segment that enhanced replicative fitness (Memoli et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Memoli et al. (2009).

claim: The phylodynamic model yields a spindly HA phylogeny with low-load viruses populating the trunk and higher load viruses populating the tips of the phylogeny.
source: When simulated under parameters appropriate for influenza A/H3N2 in humans, this model yields a spindly HA phylogeny with low-load viruses populating the trunk and higher load viruses populating the tips of the phylogeny (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylodynamic model simulations shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The distribution of deleterious mutation loads on the simulated phylogeny is consistent with the excess number of non-synonymous substitutions on external tree branches found for human influenza A/H3N2.
source: This distribution of deleterious mutation loads on the simulated phylogeny is consistent with the excess number of non-synonymous substitutions on external tree branches that was found for human influenza A/H3N2 (Fitch et al., 1997; Pybus et al., 2007) and arises because deleterious mutations contribute a substantial fraction of the fitness variance in the viral population (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations and citations to empirical studies.

claim: Deleterious mutations contribute a substantial fraction of the fitness variance in the viral population.
source: This distribution of deleterious mutation loads on the simulated phylogeny is consistent with the excess number of non-synonymous substitutions on external tree branches that was found for human influenza A/H3N2 (Fitch et al., 1997; Pybus et al., 2007) and arises because deleterious mutations contribute a substantial fraction of the fitness variance in the viral population (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The phylodynamic model simulation reproduces antigenic variant co-circulation.
source: The phylodynamic model simulation further reproduces antigenic variant co-circulation (Figures 6B, 7B), consistent with findings that lineages that are lost nevertheless undergo appreciable antigenic evolution (Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012) and that antigenic diversity levels within clusters can exceed antigenic distances between clusters (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figures 6B and 7B, and citations.

claim: The simulation yields prevalence levels of 10–180 cases per 100,000 individuals.
source: The simulation yields prevalence levels of 10–180 cases per 100,000 individuals (Figure 7B) and annual attack rates of approximately 2–10%, consistent with empirical estimates of influenza incidence (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The simulation yields annual attack rates of approximately 2–10%.
source: The simulation yields prevalence levels of 10–180 cases per 100,000 individuals (Figure 7B) and annual attack rates of approximately 2–10%, consistent with empirical estimates of influenza incidence (World Health Organization, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 7B and a citation.

claim: The trunk of the phylogeny carries low-load viruses that have a high number of susceptible hosts.
source: From these figures, it is clear that the trunk of the phylogeny carries low-load viruses (Figure 6A) that have a high number of susceptible hosts (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figures 6A and 6C.

claim: The combination of low mutation load and high number of susceptible hosts yields high-fitness viruses.
source: This combination together yields high-fitness viruses, as epidemiologically given by their net reproductive rates R (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Neither a low mutation load alone nor a high number of susceptible hosts alone suffice in generating a sufficiently high-fitness viral lineage that will ensure its long-term evolutionary success.
source: Neither a low mutation load alone nor a high number of susceptible hosts alone suffice in generating a sufficiently high-fitness viral lineage that will ensure its long-term evolutionary success.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model results.

claim: Trunk lineages abruptly gain susceptible hosts as a result of single large antigenic mutations that occur in good genetic backgrounds.
source: Inspection of Figure 6C also shows that trunk lineages abruptly gain susceptible hosts. These abrupt gains are a result of single large antigenic mutations that, when occurring in good genetic backgrounds, initiate the selective sweeps that ultimately limit influenza's genetic diversity.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The tMRCA plot from the phylodynamic model reproduces quantitative features of influenza A/H3N2's tMRCA plot presented in Bedford et al. (2011).
source: This tMRCA plot reproduces quantitative features of influenza A/H3N2's tMRCA plot presented in Bedford et al. (2011), including its interannual variation and the observed major drops in tMRCA following the emergence of new and antigenically very distinct clusters.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model results with empirical data from Bedford et al. (2011).

claim: Simulations under the assumption of no deleterious mutations very rapidly yield explosive genetic and antigenic diversity.
source: The importance of deleterious mutations in constraining the genetic and antigenic diversity of influenza can be further illustrated by simulating the phylodynamic model under the assumption of their absence. These simulations very rapidly yield explosive genetic and antigenic diversity (Figure 8A) and, as a consequence, prevalence levels that generally increase over time (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Simulations under the assumption of no deleterious mutations yield prevalence levels that generally increase over time.
source: The importance of deleterious mutations in constraining the genetic and antigenic diversity of influenza can be further illustrated by simulating the phylodynamic model under the assumption of their absence. These simulations very rapidly yield explosive genetic and antigenic diversity (Figure 8A) and, as a consequence, prevalence levels that generally increase over time (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The finding that simulations without deleterious mutations yield explosive diversity is consistent with predictions from previous influenza modeling work incorporating only strain-specific immunity.
source: Reassuringly, this finding is consistent with predictions from previous influenza modeling work incorporating only strain-specific immunity (Ferguson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferguson et al. (2003).

claim: Simulations under the assumption of no antigenic mutations gave rise to significantly higher levels of genetic diversity compared with simulations including both antigenic and deleterious mutations.
source: Given that purifying selection alone is known to reduce genetic diversity (Charlesworth et al., 1993; Walczak et al., 2012), we further simulated the phylodynamic model under the assumption of no antigenic mutations. In these simulations, we phenomenologically incorporated antigenic drift by simulating susceptible-infected-recovered-susceptible (SIRS) dynamics such that prevalence levels were similar to those shown in Figure 7B. Compared with the results shown in Figure 6, these simulations gave rise to significantly higher levels of genetic diversity (Figure 9A) and longer tMRCAs (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Purifying selection alone does not account for the spindly phylogenies shown in Figure 6.
source: This indicates that purifying selection alone does not account for the spindly phylogenies shown in Figure 6.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model simulations.

claim: It is antigenic evolution in the context of fitness variation generated by deleterious mutations that constrains the viral phylogeny.
source: Rather, it is antigenic evolution in the context of fitness variation generated by deleterious mutations that constrains the viral phylogeny.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model simulations.

claim: For λ values of 0.10 and higher, empirically documented annual attack rates can be consistently reproduced.
source: For λ values of 0.10 and higher, empirically documented annual attack rates can be consistently reproduced.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations.

claim: Maximum and minimum tMRCAs are best reproduced for λ values between 0.10 and 0.15.
source: Maximum and minimum tMRCAs are best reproduced for λ values between 0.10 and 0.15.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations.

claim: A broad range of sd values yields dynamics that are consistent with influenza A/H3N2 dynamics in humans.
source: Despite the dependency of evolutionary and epidemiological dynamics on sd, Figure 10C,D shows that a broad range of sd values yields dynamics that are consistent with influenza A/H3N2 dynamics in humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 10C,D.

claim: In the absence of antigenic evolution (λantigenic = 0), maximum tMRCAs are significantly higher than empirically documented.
source: In the absence of antigenic evolution (λantigenic = 0), maximum tMRCAs are significantly higher than empirically documented (Figure 10E) and maximum annual attack rates do not exceed 3.8% (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 10E.

claim: In the absence of antigenic evolution (λantigenic = 0), maximum annual attack rates do not exceed 3.8%.
source: In the absence of antigenic evolution (λantigenic = 0), maximum tMRCAs are significantly higher than empirically documented (Figure 10E) and maximum annual attack rates do not exceed 3.8% (Figure 10F).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 10F.

claim: It is the interaction between deleterious and advantageous immune escape mutations that consistently yields a spindly phylogeny and high annual attack rates.
source: Finally, taken together, Figure 10A,B,E,F again indicates that it is the interaction between deleterious and advantageous immune escape mutations that consistently yields a spindly phylogeny and high annual attack rates.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model simulations shown in Figure 10.

claim: Neither deleterious mutations nor immune escape mutations alone succeed in reproducing the dynamic features of influenza.
source: Neither deleterious mutations nor immune escape mutations alone succeed in reproducing these dynamic features of influenza.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model simulations.

claim: The epochal evolution model assumes that neutral or nearly neutral mutations accumulate at HA epitopes and that these changes enable a previously neutral mutation to exact a large antigenic effect.
source: Influenza's epochal evolution model (Koelle et al., 2006) assumes that neutral or nearly neutral mutations accumulate at HA epitopes and that these changes enable a previously neutral mutation to exact a large antigenic effect and thereby to precipitate an antigenic cluster transition.
evidence: This claim describes the assumptions of a cited model.

claim: Recent work indicates that amino acid changes that are responsible for cluster transitions have large antigenic effects in consensus sequences.
source: First, recent work indicates that amino acid changes that are responsible for cluster transitions have large antigenic effects in consensus sequences (Koel et al., 2013), such that genetic context is unlikely to be of utmost importance in determining the antigenic effect of mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koel et al. (2013).

claim: Positive selection acts not only between antigenic clusters but also within antigenic clusters.
source: Second, a molecular evolutionary analysis following the publication of the epochal evolution model has indicated that positive selection acts not only between antigenic clusters but also within antigenic clusters (Suzuki, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki (2008).

claim: Multiple antigenic variants co-circulate.
source: In support of this finding, a more recent statistical analysis has shown that multiple antigenic variants co-circulate (Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Strelkowa and Lässig (2012).

claim: The evolution of influenza is unlikely to be limited by the occurrence of antigenic mutations.
source: Both of these empirical analyses are inconsistent with the assumptions of the epochal evolution model and indicate that the evolution of influenza is unlikely to be limited by the occurrence of antigenic mutations.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited empirical analyses.

claim: The generalized cross-immunity model and the canalization model can reproduce influenza's spindly HA phylogeny.
source: The two other existing models that can reproduce influenza's spindly HA phylogeny are the generalized cross-immunity model put forward by Ferguson et al. (2003) and the canalization model put forward by Bedford et al. (2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ferguson et al. (2003) and Bedford et al. (2012).

claim: Both the generalized cross-immunity model and the canalization model yield antigenic variant co-circulation when simulated.
source: When simulated, both of these models yield antigenic variant co-circulation and are thus consistent with the analyses detailed above that have shown that influenza evolution is not antigenic mutation limited.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited models.

claim: In Ferguson et al. (2003), generalized (strain-transcending) cross-immunity lasting on the order of 6 months was invoked to limit the genetic and antigenic diversity of influenza A/H3N2 in humans.
source: In Ferguson et al. (2003), generalized (strain-transcending) cross-immunity lasting on the order of 6 months was invoked to limit the genetic and antigenic diversity of influenza A/H3N2 in humans.
evidence: This claim describes a feature of a cited model.

claim: There is evidence for long-lasting cross-immunity between more genetically distant strains (including heterologous influenza A subtypes), but it appears to reduce pathology and possibly accelerate viral clearance rather than prevent infection.
source: The major criticism of this model is lack of empirical support for this duration and form of generalized cross-immunity: while there is evidence for long-lasting cross-immunity between more genetically distant strains (including heterologous influenza A subtypes), it appears to reduce pathology and possibly accelerate viral clearance rather than prevent infection (Grebe et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grebe et al. (2008).

claim: A recent experimental study in ferrets indicates that generalized cross-immunity that prevents infection appears to exist, but that it lasts for less than a week.
source: A recent experimental study in ferrets indicates that generalized cross-immunity that prevents infection appears to exist, but that it lasts for less than a week (Laurie et al., 2015), which is insufficiently long to limit genetic and antigenic diversity in the model of Ferguson et al.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laurie et al. (2015).

claim: The canalization model by Bedford et al. assumes that antigenic mutations move viral strains in a two-dimensional (or higher) antigenic space.
source: The canalization model by Bedford et al. does not invoke generalized cross-immunity but instead assumes that antigenic mutations move viral strains in a two-dimensional (or higher) antigenic space.
evidence: This claim describes a feature of a cited model.

claim: Models that start with the assumption of antigenic maps considerably inflate the degree of competition between antigenic variants.
source: While these antigenic spaces or maps have been used to visualize the trajectories of flu's antigenic evolution (Smith et al., 2004; de Jong et al., 2007), models that start with the assumption of these maps considerably inflate the degree of competition between antigenic variants.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about model assumptions and citations.

claim: Antigenic distances between daughter variants are necessarily subadditive in antigenic space.
source: This inflation of competition results from antigenic distances between daughter variants (variants that are produced from the same parent) necessarily being subadditive in this space.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the mathematical properties of antigenic space.

claim: An increase in the fitness variance of a population acts to slow adaptive evolution and make the characteristic size of adaptive mutations that fix larger.
source: From the population genetics literature on asexual populations in which interference effects are at play, it is well known that an increase in the fitness variance of a population acts to slow adaptive evolution and make the characteristic size of adaptive mutations that fix larger.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from population genetics literature.

claim: Beneficial mutations can contribute to inherited variation in fitness.
source: While here we have invoked deleterious mutations in the generation of fitness variation, beneficial mutations can similarly contribute to inherited variation in fitness (Birky and Walsh, 1988; Barton, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to population genetics literature.

claim: Interference between beneficial mutations (or a combination of beneficial and deleterious mutations) similarly slows down the rate of adaptive evolution and increases the size of adaptive mutants that fix.
source: Thus, in population genetic models, interference between beneficial mutations (or a combination of beneficial and deleterious mutations) similarly slows down the rate of adaptive evolution and increases the size of adaptive mutants that fix (Birky and Walsh, 1988; Barton, 1995; Gerrish and Lenski, 1998; Rouzine et al., 2003, 2008; Park et al., 2010; Sniegowski and Gerrish, 2010; Schiffels et al., 2011; Good et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to population genetics literature.

claim: Antigenic changes allow for escape from herd immunity and by definition reduce competition for susceptible hosts.
source: In the context of influenza, however, it is a change in antigenicity that is thought to provide the selective advantage. Because antigenic changes allow for escape from herd immunity, these changes by definition reduce competition for susceptible hosts (the virus resource).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from epidemiological principles.

claim: Antigenic mutants create a partially new niche and so do not necessarily lead to competitive exclusion.
source: As such, antigenic mutants create a partially new niche and so do not necessarily lead to competitive exclusion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from epidemiological principles.

claim: The establishment of antigenic mutants can lead to long-term coexistence and a larger infected population size.
source: The establishment of antigenic mutants can therefore instead lead to long-term coexistence and, as a result of only partial cross-immunity, a larger infected population size.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from epidemiological principles.

claim: Explosive genetic and antigenic diversity is expected in the presence of only strain-specific immunity.
source: This is why explosive genetic and antigenic diversity is expected in the presence of only strain-specific immunity (Ferguson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ferguson et al. (2003).

claim: Generalized cross-immunity acts to considerably increase the competition between strains for susceptible hosts.
source: In this context, generalized cross-immunity acts to considerably increase the competition between strains for susceptible hosts (as well as to reduce the overall infected population size).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from epidemiological principles.

claim: The deleterious mutation model does not need to invoke processes to augment competition between antigenic strains because a large proportion of fitness variation in the virus population arises from differences in deleterious mutation loads.
source: In contrast, the deleterious mutation model we present here does not need to invoke processes to augment competition between antigenic strains because a large proportion of fitness variation in the virus population arises from differences in deleterious mutation loads (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model results shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The deleterious mutation model can reproduce empirically observed high annual attack rates on the order of 10–15%.
source: As such, our model can reproduce empirically observed high annual attack rates on the order of 10–15% (Figure 10B for λ = 0.10).
evidence: This claim is supported by model simulations shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The deleterious mutation model provides a more plausible mechanistic explanation for influenza's characteristic evolutionary features than other models.
source: Because deleterious mutations are known to circulate in the influenza A/H3N2 virus population (Fitch et al., 1997; Pybus et al., 2007; Strelkowa and Lässig, 2012), and in light of existing criticisms of the other two models, we therefore argue that the model presented here provides a more plausible mechanistic explanation for influenza's characteristic evolutionary features.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model results, citations, and comparison with other models.

claim: Cellular receptor binding avidity is an important phenotype that impacts viral fitness.
source: One such finding is that cellular receptor binding avidity is an important phenotype that impacts viral fitness (Hensley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hensley et al. (2009).

claim: In a naive host, influenza viruses with low receptor binding avidities have a selective advantage.
source: In a naive host, influenza viruses with low receptor binding avidities have a selective advantage, whereas, in a more immune host, influenza viruses with high receptor binding avidities have a selective advantage (Hensley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hensley et al. (2009).

claim: In a more immune host, influenza viruses with high receptor binding avidities have a selective advantage.
source: In a naive host, influenza viruses with low receptor binding avidities have a selective advantage, whereas, in a more immune host, influenza viruses with high receptor binding avidities have a selective advantage (Hensley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hensley et al. (2009).

claim: Changes in receptor binding avidity frequently also alter antigenicity.
source: Because changes in receptor binding avidity frequently also alter antigenicity (Hensley et al., 2009), it is therefore also easily conceivable that certain of these changes increase virus fitness via two distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hensley et al. (2009).

claim: Successful cluster transitions via the 'jackpot' strategy may preferentially involve mutations that simultaneously affect binding avidity and antigenicity.
source: Successful cluster transitions via the 'jackpot' strategy, as depicted in Figure 2C, may therefore preferentially involve mutations that simultaneously affect binding avidity and antigenicity.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation and inference from model results and cited work.

claim: The majority of cluster-transition mutations fall near the receptor binding site of influenza's HA.
source: Indeed, the majority of cluster-transition mutations that have been recently characterized fall near the receptor binding site of influenza's HA (Koel et al., 2013), suggesting that changes in the receptor binding avidity phenotype that occur with these antigenic mutations may improve virus fitness.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koel et al. (2013).

claim: Glycosylation of influenza's HA is known to impact virus fitness.
source: In addition to cellular receptor binding avidity, glycosylation of influenza's HA is known to impact virus fitness.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge.

claim: Glycosylation sites accumulate over evolutionary time in H3N2 in humans.
source: Whether glycosylation sites accumulate over evolutionary time (as in the case of H3N2 in humans [Blackburne et al., 2008]) or do not (as in the case of H1N1 in humans [Das et al., 2011]) therefore will depend on how these sites impact the background fitness of virus strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Blackburne et al. (2008).

claim: Glycosylation sites do not accumulate over evolutionary time in H1N1 in humans.
source: Whether glycosylation sites accumulate over evolutionary time (as in the case of H3N2 in humans [Blackburne et al., 2008]) or do not (as in the case of H1N1 in humans [Das et al., 2011]) therefore will depend on how these sites impact the background fitness of virus strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Das et al. (2011).

claim: In H1N1, glycosylation has been shown to significantly reduce receptor binding avidity and therewith to lower overall virus fitness.
source: In the case of H1N1, for example, glycosylation has been shown to significantly reduce receptor binding avidity and therewith to lower overall virus fitness, despite the beneficial effect of glycosylation on escape from antibody-mediated neutralization (Das et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Das et al. (2011).

claim: Compensatory mutations are needed to restore virus fitness following the addition of a glycosylation site in H1N1.
source: Compensatory mutations are therefore needed to restore virus fitness following the addition of a glycosylation site (Das et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Das et al. (2011).

claim: Circulation of deleterious mutations has been established in a wide range of RNA viruses.
source: Beyond the influenza viruses, circulation of deleterious mutations has been established in a wide range of RNA viruses (Pybus et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pybus et al. (2007).

claim: Punctuated antigenic evolution has been documented for norovirus.
source: One especially intriguing case is that of norovirus, for which punctuated antigenic evolution has been documented (Lindesmith et al., 2008, 2011) and for which deleterious mutations along with differential binding to histoblood group antigens may contribute to fitness variation (Donaldson et al., 2008; Lindesmith et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lindesmith et al. (2008, 2011).

claim: For norovirus, deleterious mutations along with differential binding to histoblood group antigens may contribute to fitness variation.
source: One especially intriguing case is that of norovirus, for which punctuated antigenic evolution has been documented (Lindesmith et al., 2008, 2011) and for which deleterious mutations along with differential binding to histoblood group antigens may contribute to fitness variation (Donaldson et al., 2008; Lindesmith et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Donaldson et al. (2008) and Lindesmith et al. (2008).

claim: Two recent publications have made great strides in predicting the genetic evolution of influenza A/H3N2 in humans over the short term.
source: Indeed, two recent publications have made great strides in predicting the genetic evolution of influenza A/H3N2 in humans over the short term (Neher et al., 2014; Łuksza and Lässig, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Neher et al. (2014) and Łuksza and Lässig (2014).

claim: Łuksza and Lässig's approach incorporated knowledge of antigenic and non-antigenic sites in developing a fitness model for influenza A/H3N2.
source: Łuksza and Lässig's approach incorporated knowledge of antigenic and non-antigenic sites in developing a fitness model for this virus.
evidence: This claim describes a feature of cited work.

claim: With the assumption that mutations at non-antigenic sites were weakly deleterious, Łuksza and Lässig were able to predict which influenza clades would grow and which ones would decline with an accuracy of 93% and 76%, respectively.
source: With the assumption that mutations at non-antigenic sites were weakly deleterious, the authors were able to predict which influenza clades would grow and which ones would decline with an accuracy of 93% and 76%, respectively (Koelle and Rasmussen, 2014; Łuksza and Lässig, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koelle and Rasmussen (2014) and Łuksza and Lässig (2014).

claim: Neher et al.'s approach relied on branching patterns present in the HA phylogeny to predict strain evolution, with a success rate comparable to that of Łuksza and Lässig.
source: Instead of using knowledge specific to influenza A/H3N2, Neher et al.'s approach relied on branching patterns present in the HA phylogeny to predict strain evolution, with a success rate comparable to that of Łuksza and Lässig.
evidence: This claim describes a feature of cited work.

claim: The ability of both prediction models to predict influenza evolution rests on the presence of substantial fitness variation in the influenza A/H3N2 virus population.
source: The ability of both of these models to predict influenza evolution rests on the presence of substantial fitness variation in the influenza A/H3N2 virus population.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited work.

claim: Cluster transitions will only succeed when large antigenic mutations find themselves in good genetic backgrounds, which must be largely determined by non-antigenic phenotypes.
source: The work here contributes to this understanding by reconciling the presence of fitness variation in the virus population with the observation of limited genetic and antigenic diversity of influenza A/H3N2's HA in the long run: cluster transitions will only succeed when large antigenic mutations find themselves in good genetic backgrounds, which must be largely determined by non-antigenic phenotypes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from model results.

claim: Successfully predicting cluster transitions will require better characterizing the antigenic effects of mutations and characterizing relative virus fitness.
source: Successfully predicting cluster transitions will therefore require not only better characterizing the antigenic effects of mutations but also characterizing relative virus fitness, as mediated by differential deleterious mutation loads and contributions of non-antigenic phenotypes, in influenza's HA and other gene segments.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about future research needs.

claim: The deleterious mutation-selection balance is given by a Poisson distribution with mean λ/sd.
source: In an explicit susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR) epidemiological context that does not yet incorporate immune escape, these assumptions lead to a deleterious mutation-selection balance in the virus population ('Materials and methods', Figure 1A). This balance is given by a Poisson distribution with mean λ/sd, where λ is per-genome deleterious mutation rate and sd is the transmission fitness cost of sublethal deleterious mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by mathematical derivation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Within-host fitness costs of 0.103–0.132 yield transmission fitness costs between 0.002 and 0.018, with a mean transmission fitness cost sd of 0.008.
source: For them, we found that within-host fitness costs of 0.103–0.132 yielded transmission fitness costs between 0.002 and 0.018, with a mean transmission fitness cost sd of 0.008, which we use in Figure 1A–C.
evidence: This claim is supported by calculations based on within-host model simulations and cited empirical estimates.

claim: Influenza B has a lower mutation rate than influenza A/H3N2.
source: For example, influenza B is known to have a lower mutation rate than influenza A/H3N2 (Nobusawa and Sato, 2006; Sanjuán et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nobusawa and Sato (2006) and Sanjuán et al. (2010).

claim: Influenza B evolves antigenically in a less punctuated manner than influenza A/H3N2.
source: Our model would therefore predict that influenza B evolves antigenically in a less punctuated manner than influenza A/H3N2—a pattern that has been recently documented (Bedford et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a model prediction and a citation to Bedford et al. (2014).

claim: Influenza B has a slower rate of antigenic evolution than influenza A/H3N2.
source: However, a lower mutation rate would also surely reduce the rate at which antigenic mutations occur. The slower rate of antigenic evolution observed for influenza B (Bedford et al., 2014) is therefore not inconsistent with our model.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bedford et al. (2014).

claim: Human influenza A/H1N1 shows a similar pattern to H3N2 in terms of punctuated antigenic evolution.
source: Relative to these two influenza viruses, human influenza A/H1N1 shows a similar pattern to H3N2 in terms of punctuated antigenic evolution (Bedford et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bedford et al. (2014).

claim: H1N1's rate of antigenic evolution is considerably slower than H3N2's, although it is faster than influenza B's rate of antigenic evolution.
source: Despite this similarity, H1N1's rate of antigenic evolution is considerably slower than H3N2's, although it is faster than influenza B's rate of antigenic evolution (Bedford et al., 2014, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bedford et al. (2014, 2015).

claim: H1N1 appears to experience weaker antigenic selection than H3N2 in humans.
source: This explanation is consistent with the finding that H1N1 appears to experience weaker antigenic selection than H3N2 in humans (Bhatt et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bhatt et al. (2011).

claim: Swine influenza A/H3N2 evolves genetically at a rate that is similar to that of human influenza A/H3N2.
source: For example, the same H3N2 virus that is circulating in humans emerged in pigs in the early 1970s. This swine influenza A/H3N2 evolves genetically at a rate that is similar to that of human influenza A/H3N2 (de Jong et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to de Jong et al. (2007).

claim: Swine influenza A/H3N2's rate of antigenic evolution is approximately six times slower than the same virus's in humans.
source: However, its rate of antigenic evolution is approximately six times slower than the same virus's in humans (de Jong et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to de Jong et al. (2007).
